structure.title: 2. Territorial control in postcolonial African states
3. Brief background of the DRC's efforts to assert the state
4. Constructing a dataset on armed group violence in conflict
5.1 The causal effect of Kimia II (design, estimates, robustness)
5.2 Characterizing the effect (reporting bias, falsification, duration, samples)
6. Better to build states through bargain? The Sun City peace agreement

observations.statement: The main design is a single-date event study with village and province-year fixed effects, estimated with the Borusyak et al. imputation estimator; treatment is an indicator for villages controlled by the rebel group in the year before the operation, interacted with event-time indicators.

Three setting features are argued to support identification: overwhelming military asymmetry (treatment not bundled with army violence), no consolidation of state control afterwards, and an externally driven decision (a concession to a foreign government) that makes reverse causality unlikely.

The hypothesis is stated as a one-sided test that post-event coefficients are positive; pre-period coefficients are inspected for pre-trends with the reference group described explicitly in the figure notes.
observations.quote: We seek to test whether βk > 0, k > 0.

observations.statement: A footnote justifies the estimator choice: with simultaneous (non-staggered) treatment most recent DiD estimators offer no gain over OLS, while the chosen imputation estimator is argued to be efficient and robust to pre-testing; other estimators are reported in the authors' supplementary appendix as giving the same conclusions.

A two-period DiD version (equation 2) is presented as a secondary specification; because the panel spans earlier wars, a control for treated villages interacted with the post-2004 window is added to separate the operation's effect from the earlier creation of the rebel-controlled area.

The same event-study equation is re-used for a second policy (a peace agreement) by swapping the treatment indicator and event date, so the two state-building strategies are analysed with a common template.

The core data are an author-built village-year panel of armed-group attacks reconstructed from household surveys, village experts and qualitative interviews in two provinces; collection rounds and years are stated, and the panel covers attacks recalled since the mid-1990s.

Authors define named samples (quasi-experimental window, confounding villages, quasi-experimental villages) and exclude one district's villages from the baseline because a later troop redeployment there created a documented security vacuum; pre-period characteristics of excluded versus retained villages are compared in an appendix table.
observations.locator: Section 4, last paragraph; Supplementary Table B.1

observations.statement: Every table and event-study figure note reports the number of village-year observations and the number of clusters at each clustering level.

To study persistence, a second data collection in 2022 revisited a subset of the original villages plus additional villages chosen to raise statistical power; the recall window used is restricted to years judged reliably recallable, and the resource constraint behind the subset choice is stated.

Public conflict-event data (ACLED) and a peace-agreement database (PA-X) are used for cross-country descriptive event studies and as an external check on the author-collected data; the paper notes ACLED's coarse geolocation in the study area and the bandwidth used to link events to villages.
A footnote describes enumerator backgrounds, prior training and experience, and the additional training and piloting for qualitative recall techniques.

The outcome is a village-year indicator for an attack by the targeted group; treatment is control by that group in the year before the operation. Attack motive categories (pillage, conquest, punishment) are taken from villagers' own taxonomy, with the pillage indicator broadened to include abduction or confiscation of wealth.
Household-level targeting proxies (political exposure, wealth) are combined into normalized indices constructed by principal component analysis, reported alongside the individual components.
observations.locator: Table 2 Panels B and C notes

observations.statement: Motive classification is validated against observable attack characteristics in an appendix table; a value comparison is reported with and without winsorizing the top of the distribution; count and inverse hyperbolic sine transformations of attacks are used as alternative outcomes.
observations.locator: Section 5.1.3 last paragraph; Section 5.3.1; Supplementary Tables B.3, B.8

observations.statement: Income and asset denominators for the tax-burden benchmark are reconstructed in a footnote from a perpetual inventory of livestock and from gold-mining productivity, prices, and workforce shares, with each input's source or assumption listed.

Main tables report the DiD coefficient with clustered SE, observations, R2, the pre-treatment treated-group mean of the dependent variable, cluster counts at both levels, and a Conley spatial-SE p-value row; fixed effects and stars conventions are described in the notes.

Each table's first column repeats the baseline estimate as a benchmark; later columns vary the dependent variable (by motive or by welfare cost) and add controls for other motives or interaction terms, with rows of Y/N indicators for included controls.

For triple-interaction household regressions, a final column reports the fully saturated model including all lower-order interaction terms, and the notes state that coefficients not reported are controls.
observations.locator: Section 5.3.1; Table 2 Panels B and C

observations.statement: Standard errors are two-way clustered at village and chiefdom-year; cluster counts are given in a footnote, and Monte Carlo simulations in the authors' supplementary appendix are cited as showing the two-way clustered SEs of the imputation estimator perform well in finite samples.

In the smaller persistence samples the notes acknowledge fewer clusters may cause over-rejection, cite a rule of thumb from the clustering literature, and report that alternative clustering (village and groupement-year) and no clustering give identical results in the supplementary appendix.

Conley spatial standard errors (fixed radius, AR(1)) are reported as a p-value row in every table and with varying spatial assumptions in an appendix figure; a permutation exercise re-assigning treated status across villages many times is used to compute a sharp-null p-value.
observations.locator: Footnotes 7 and 8; Table 1 notes; Supplementary Figures B.5, B.7

observations.statement: A footnote describes simulating random misclassification of the binary outcome at several levels, re-estimating many times and combining estimates with multiple-imputation style variance formulas, to find the error level at which the result would disappear.

Pre-trend coefficients are plotted in the main event-study figure; notes explain that pre-trends are estimated in a separate regression with a distinct reference group, which explains the visual gap between the last pre and first post coefficient.

Pre-treatment characteristics of treated versus other villages, and of excluded versus retained villages, are tabulated in the appendix; a further appendix table reports predicted treatment probability by covariate.
observations.locator: Section 5.1.1; Supplementary Tables B.1, B.4; Footnote 6

observations.statement: A falsification figure in the main text re-runs the event study with attacks by other armed actors as the outcome, both in treated villages and in villages controlled by other actors, to check that the operation did not change general violence dynamics.
Appendix figures re-estimate the DiD using each year in a window as the placebo event date, and using each chiefdom in turn as the placebo treated area.

Before regressions, descriptive figures show territorial control over time and raw time series of attack rates for treated and other villages, so the reader sees the treatment actually occurred and the raw pattern behind the estimates.

A single appendix table collects DiD robustness columns: adding excluded villages, district-year fixed effects, village linear trends, baseline covariates interacted with year dummies, migration controls, all combined, a gold-village subsample, Conley SEs, and a public-data replication; the text discusses which columns move the estimate and why.

Because the baseline is a linear probability model, logit, conditional logit, count and IHS-count versions are reported in an appendix table, motivated by measurement-error concerns cited from the literature.

A long footnote lists further checks: replacing fixed effects with indicators, dropping one chiefdom, alternative cluster levels, mineral price interactions, distance-to-treated-area interactions, and lagged dependent variable instead of village fixed effects.

A dedicated subsection addresses consistency across data sources and samples, with one appendix table estimating the DiD on the original sample, the geographic subset, the newly collected data, the expanded sample, pooled samples, and the universe of villages in the treated chiefdom.

Reporting bias is addressed in four steps: replication with public data, an analytical bound on how much over-reporting would be needed to overturn the result, a simulation of that bound, and interviews with perpetrators reporting the same pattern.
observations.locator: Section 5.2.1; Supplementary Section C.1, Figure B.9

observations.statement: Heterogeneity is used only as mechanism evidence: treatment is interacted with lagged army presence at the village level, and with household political-exposure or wealth proxies in household-year data, to distinguish war, retaliation and theft explanations.

Mechanism section decomposes attacks by purported motive, rules out war and retaliation via perpetrator identity and within-village targeting, cross-checks with perpetrator interviews, presents a simple model in the appendix, computes a break-even horizon for the taxation versus pillage trade-off, and tests an income-effect alternative using villages with low expropriation frequency.

The explanation for why the effect ends is explicitly labelled suggestive because the quasi-experiment is the operation's completion rather than later state consolidation; it rests on combatant interviews and a descriptive appendix figure.
observations.quote: would hinge on weak empirical grounds

observations.statement: Block quotes from village qualitative reports and secondary literature are interleaved with quantitative results throughout, with longer qualitative material relegated to lettered appendix sections.
observations.locator: Sections 5.1.1, 5.2.4, 6.2; Supplementary Sections A.1 to A.4

observations.statement: Effects are interpreted as changes from the pre-treatment treated mean, converted to per-village and per-household monetary amounts, benchmarked as tax burden shares of assets and income, and combined into a statement of the compensation villagers would need to accept for the welfare trade-off.

When sample size changes across columns or figures, the text notes wider confidence intervals or the different sample explicitly, and cautions that coefficient changes across subsamples are unsurprising.

Cross-country correlations in Section 2 are explicitly called correlational and motivating only; the peace-agreement comparison is flagged as covering a different period and different groups and framed as a benchmark 'possibility result' rather than a clean comparison.

Authors acknowledge that their own recall data may be biased and that the public data are poorly geolocated in the study area, and describe the corrections they made to the public data in the supplementary appendix.

The conclusion separates which costs are specific to how this state bargained (army positions) from which are general (signalling that extortion pays), and offers comparative statics on when each strategy is more desirable.

Figures include maps of territorial control, raw time series paired with event-study coefficient plots with confidence bands, and figure notes that state the sample size, cluster levels and counts, the estimator and the reference group.

Tables use three-level significance stars, put SEs in parentheses, and add a Conley p-value row rather than a second SE row; notes define each dependent variable per column and explain the mean-of-dependent row.

Descriptive statistics are placed in the supplementary appendix (Table B.1) and summarized in prose in the main text; appendix material is split into lettered sections (A qualitative, B tables and figures, C derivations and model) plus separate authors' personal appendices.

The introduction previews the four analytical steps and their outcomes, then gives a three-point contribution paragraph and a policy-implications paragraph; the data section precedes the design and estimating equation.

Empirical order is: descriptive context, main event study, a short robustness subsection, a 'characterizing the effect' section (reporting bias, falsification, duration, sample consistency), mechanisms, welfare, then the comparison policy; most robustness tables and figures live in the appendix and are referenced from footnotes.

A motivating cross-country section using public conflict and peace-agreement data precedes the case study; its role is stated as descriptive comparison and the limits of that evidence are used to motivate the disaggregated design.
A data availability statement cites a Zenodo replication package by DOI; supplementary data are stated to be available at the journal website. No software is named in the main text.

Primary data were collected by the authors' own research organisation over several fieldwork rounds; armed-group lifespans were compiled from online trackers, secondary sources and hired local informants, documented in a separate authors' appendix.
The acknowledgments include a note explaining and disclaiming the normative baggage of the term 'rebels' as used throughout the paper.

gaps: No explicit justification for the choice of chiefdom-year (rather than another level) as the second clustering dimension beyond the Monte Carlo reference.
No software or package named in the main text; the replication package is cited only by DOI.
No ethics, IRB or consent statement despite household surveys and interviews with armed-group members.
Summary statistics table is not in the main text (appendix only).
No multiple-testing adjustment discussed for the many outcomes in Tables 2 and 3.
Online supplementary appendix and authors' personal appendices are not in the text file, so appendix practices are known only from in-text references.

reading.note: All 31 pages of the published article read, including tables, figure notes, footnotes, acknowledgments, data availability statement and references. The supplementary appendix (Sections A, B, C) and the authors' personal supplementary appendices I and II are separate documents not included in the text file and were not read.
